 GM 6.2L V8 engine failures: Which years are affected?
 Tim Esterdahl 
 Tim Esterdahl
 Tim Esterdahl 
 | November 18, 2026 | 0 comments Tim Esterdahl
 | November 18, 2026
 | 0 comments
 Chevrolet’s L87 6.2-liter V8 is shown in this file image, not the specific engine torn down by Dave’s Auto Center. (Photo courtesy of Chevrolet) 
 If you’re shopping for a used Silverado, Sierra or full-size GM SUV, it’s fair to ask which years you should worry about. The GM 6.2L V8 engine failures involve a specific engine, the L87. Certain 2021–2024 vehicles are recalled, but federal investigators are also looking at earlier and later trucks. A clean recall search tells you whether there’s an open recall on that VIN. It doesn’t tell you whether that model year is under investigation.
 This is a different issue from the 5.3L V8 lifter failures we covered . The 6.2L recall centers on crankshaft and connecting-rod defects that can damage bearings and cause engine failure and loss of propulsion. Here’s where the model years fall, and how the aftermarket is looking into solutions, including Dave’s Auto Center.
 2021–2024: Which 6.2L V8s GM recalled
 2021 GMC Sierra 1500. Only certain trucks equipped with the L87 are covered by this recall. (Photo courtesy of General Motors) 
 GM’s amended U.S. recall filing (25V-274) lists 597,571 vehicles with suspect L87 engines produced from March 1, 2021, through May 31, 2024. It covers certain Chevy Silverado 1500, Tahoe and Suburban models; GMC Sierra 1500, Yukon and Yukon XL models; and Cadillac Escalade and Escalade ESV models. Those are engine-production dates. Two trucks from the same model year may have different recall status.
 GM traced the recall defect to manufacturing problems: debris on connecting rods or in crankshaft oil passages, and crankshafts with dimensions or surface finishes outside specification. Dealers inspect the engine and repair or replace it if necessary. Engines that pass get higher-viscosity oil, a new oil filter and fill cap, and updated owner’s manual information. Eligible vehicles also get special coverage for failures tied to the listed defect : 10 years or 150,000 miles from original in-service date, whichever comes first. That is not a blanket engine warranty.
 2019–2020 and 2025–2026: Not recalled, still under investigation
 A 2020 GMC Sierra SLT. The 2019–2020 Sierra and Silverado pickups with the L87 are outside the recall but remain under federal investigation. (Photo courtesy of General Motors) 
 The 2019 and 2020 Silverado 1500 and Sierra 1500 with the L87 are outside the recall. They are, however, listed in NHTSA’s separate bearing-failure investigation, EA25007 , alongside certain 2021 and 2024 vehicles outside the recall.
 The 2025 and 2026 models are not in the existing recall either. They are part of NHTSA’s newer investigation, EA26005 , which lists an estimated 997,743 model-year 2021–2026 vehicles. The agency is looking at failures after recall work as well as failures in engines built after the original cutoff. The Nov. 13 deadline was for records from GM. It was not a deadline for repairs or a decision on expanding the recall.
 Which GM 6.2L V8s are outside these cases?
 The next-generation 2027 GMC Sierra 1500 moves to new V8s. That change does not apply across GM’s full-size SUV lineup. (Photo by Tim Esterdahl) 
 The older 6.2L L86 in vehicles such as the 2014–2018 Silverado 1500 is a different engine and isn’t covered by these L87 actions. The redesigned 2027 Silverado 1500 and Sierra 1500 use new 5.7L and 6.6L V8s, not the L87. Don’t apply that rule to the SUVs: Chevy still lists a 6.2L V8 in the 2027 Tahoe , and 2027 models aren’t listed in these federal cases. Outside the scope means just that. It doesn’t guarantee an engine won’t fail.
 The aftermarket is looking into solutions
 Dave discusses crankshaft finish and oil pressure during an L87 teardown. (Video still: Dave’s Auto Center) 
 The aftermarket is looking into solutions, too, including Dave’s Auto Center. In his Oct. 8 teardown , Dave argues that low oil pressure under light load and waviness on the crankshaft’s bearing surfaces may work together to break down the thin film of oil that keeps the parts from touching. His idea is to change how the existing variable-displacement pump is controlled so it keeps pressure higher under light loads. In a second teardown on Oct. 27 , he shows more bearing damage on another L87.
 Dave has discussed testing the idea on a dyno and looking at oil samples and bearings afterward. I haven’t seen published durability results showing that the change prevents these failures. It’s not GM’s recall remedy, and the shop’s listed L87 remanufactured long block , which removes Dynamic Fuel Management, is a separate product. That listing isn’t evidence that changing pump control fixes the bearing problem.
 What I’d check before buying a used GM 6.2L
 Before buying a Tahoe or another GM truck or SUV with a 6.2L V8, check its VIN and ask for the service records. (Photo courtesy of General Motors) 
 Start with the engine code and NHTSA’s VIN lookup . Then ask a GM dealer to check the VIN for repair history and special coverage. If the seller says the recall was done, ask for the repair order. I’d want to know whether it got the oil service or a replacement engine, and at what mileage. Our used 6.2L truck checklist walks through what to ask for. I wouldn’t treat a 2019, 2020, 2025 or 2026 as a safe bet just because it wasn’t recalled.
